scenario: AITA for telling my sister that her beating breast cancer was not impressive and not inspirational? | Three years ago my older sister was diagnosed with breast cancer. Within six months her cancer was cleared. She had minor radiAtion and then hormone therapy afterwards. She is 100% fine and healthy no need for surgery. She has since plastered it all over social media. I don’t mind it because I can choose to ignore it. But this holiday season she was insufferable. My sister walked out of the room. I thought my family would back me up but instead my parents backed up my sister. My dad didn’t say anything but he was on my sisters side. I don’t know maybe what I said wasn’t the nicest way but I don’t think I was wrong in what I said.

prediction.raw: 1. By minimizing her experience and telling her it's not impressive or inspirational, especially during a family gathering and in response to your father's health concerns, you came across as insensitive and dismissive of her feelings. It's understandable that you might feel frustrated with her constant reminders about her cancer survival, but addressing this issue in a more empathetic and less confrontational manner would have been more appropriate. Your family's reaction, with your parents backing up your sister, suggests that they perceived your comment as hurtful and inappropriate. It might be helpful to reflect on why your sister feels the need to share her story so frequently and to consider having a more nuanced and respectful conversation with her about your feelings and concerns.
